title: When you say the wrong thing
description: Everyone puts a foot wrong in conversation sometimes; what matters is the next thirty seconds.

body.heading: Stop digging
paragraphs: The first rule of saying the wrong thing is to stop explaining it. Long defences — “I only meant…”, “You have to admit it sounded like…” — turn a small stumble into a long trench.
A short, clean sentence works better: “That came out wrong. I’m sorry.” Then quiet. Let the apology be the whole message.

body.heading: Name it, do not dramatise it
paragraphs: A brief acknowledgement beats both silence and theatre. Pretending nothing happened forces the other person to carry the moment alone; making it enormous forces them to comfort you about your own mistake.
Aim for the middle: name what you said, own it, and move the conversation gently on. Most people are relieved to be handed that exit.

body.heading: Learn the shape of it
paragraphs: Later, in private, it is worth asking what the stumble was made of: tiredness, a joke borrowed from the wrong company, an assumption you did not know you held. That is where the actual repair to yourself happens.
You will say the wrong thing again. The goal is not perfection; it is becoming someone whose mistakes are small, owned, and quickly mended.

takeaway: Stop, name it, apologise once and cleanly — then learn its shape for next time.
